title: Why Seoul’s AI-exposed occupations gained jobs even as younger workers lost ground
summary: Korea’s most AI-exposed offices have so far added jobs, but an entry-level worker or an investor in regional manufacturing would draw a different conclusion from the headline. In a Bank of Korea issue note, Bosung Kim, Minsu Chung, Yujeong Jeong and Subin Jang distinguish software that generates content, agents that carry out a workflow and systems that perform physical tasks. Where those technologies can be used differs sharply across Korea. So does the region’s ability to adopt them. The early employment evidence points to concentration in the Seoul metropolitan area, which includes Incheon and Gyeonggi, alongside a nationwide difficulty for younger workers in the most exposed jobs.

The authors’ exposure measures capture tasks a technology could perform. On pages 5–6 they reduce generative exposure where supervision matters, discount agentic exposure when a person must intervene to finish a workflow, and give physical automation less weight outside controlled settings. Each measure is scaled from zero to one. Clerks, sales staff and professionals are highly exposed to generative AI, managers lead in agentic exposure, and machine operators and elementary workers are more exposed to physical automation. Professionals account for 28.1% of metropolitan employment versus 18.0% elsewhere. Equipment and machine operators make up 12.0% outside the metropolitan area versus 8.1% inside it. These differences give identical technology a different initial reach.

Employment in highly generative-exposed occupations rose by 247,000 over the three years beginning in 2023. The metropolitan area accounted for 199,000 of those jobs. During 2025 it contributed 93,000 of the 105,000 jobs added in occupations highly exposed to agents. For generative AI, a 0.1 increase in the exposure score was associated with a one percentage point higher employment growth rate in the metropolitan area, with no statistically significant relationship elsewhere. The comparable post-2025 employment interaction for agentic exposure is larger in the metropolitan area but statistically insignificant in Table 5. Those headcounts and regressions therefore provide different strengths of evidence. Neither measures how many positions firms created because they bought AI.

Vacancies and pay reveal something headcounts conceal. Employers reported more difficulty hiring for agentic-exposed jobs in the metropolitan area. Figures 17 and 19 and Table 8 also show signs of faster wage growth there. One interpretation is a scarcity of people who can deploy the tools and exercise judgment. Employment among people in their twenties in highly exposed generative and agentic work nevertheless declined in both areas. A region can gain experienced employment while offering fewer routes into an occupation. For physical AI the backdrop is different again. Highly exposed jobs have been shrinking for years, making it especially difficult to isolate a recent technology effect.

Whether AI reinforces Seoul’s advantage depends partly on which investments follow. Figure 25 puts Seoul and Gyeonggi ahead on readiness, while a large share of knowledge services and semiconductor employment is already concentrated there. But more intelligent machinery could bring engineering and research closer to manufacturing sites outside the capital. Tools that transfer expertise could also raise productivity in locally supplied services where skills are scarce. The authors propose building specialised services around regional industry, supporting regional start-ups and concentrating university investment in selected hubs. For a regional investment thesis, the evidence to seek is whether local sites begin to employ designers, technicians and service specialists as well as equipment operators.

questions.question: Do firms that actually adopt AI increase skilled hiring relative to comparable firms that do not?
questions.detail: The report ranks occupations by potential use, which can coincide with an industry upswing or stronger regional demand. Match adoption dates to vacancies, wages and headcounts within the same occupation and region. Reproducing the generative relationship within adopting firms, and observing a clearer agentic result after a longer period than Table 5 covers, would materially strengthen the interpretation.

questions.question: Where can younger workers acquire the experience that metropolitan employers appear willing to pay for?
questions.detail: Track hires, promotions and departures by age within exposed occupations alongside vacancy duration. The decline for people in their twenties and the strength of overall employment could reflect fewer junior openings, different occupation choices or faster progression out of one group. Evidence on trainee hiring and advancement would help distinguish a thinning entry pipeline from a temporary change in composition.

questions.question: Which local investments turn physical AI exposure into better regional employment?
questions.detail: Compare manufacturing locations that add engineering, software and maintenance functions with locations that only automate existing lines. Figure 25 and the readiness components in Table 11 give a starting point for matching places with similar skills and infrastructure. Sustained local growth in those higher-skilled occupations and lower youth outflows would support the proposed opportunity more convincingly than equipment purchases alone.
